claims.text: A rapid, transient thermal condition synchronizes reduction and nucleation of multiple metal species.
Synchronized reduction and nucleation allow atomic intermixing to outpace elemental segregation.
Differences in reduction potential and diffusion kinetics drive the natural tendency toward elemental segregation.
The proposed starting material is a mixture of soluble salts or complexes of multiple noble metals held in close spatial proximity.
A rapid thermal pulse can reach a regime in which all metal species reduce simultaneously.
Immediate quenching freezes the compositionally mixed state.
An inert atmosphere minimizes oxidation during the process.
Tuning ramp rate and peak temperature can trigger near-simultaneous multimetal reduction and nucleation.
Nanoscale nuclei formed during rapid thermal activation provide sites for immediate incorporation of all metal species.
A rapid thermal pulse leaves insufficient time for disparate reduction kinetics and diffusion-driven segregation to produce phase separation.
Synchronized reduction and nucleation produce a metastable homogeneous alloy before slower atomic rearrangements occur.
An optimized rapid thermal pulse will produce single-phase nanoparticles with evenly distributed elemental constituents.
A slower or uncontrolled thermal ramp allows kinetic differences to manifest and therefore produces elemental segregation and phase-separated structures.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles made from closely matched precursors under inert atmospheres.
The mechanism may not apply when reduction potentials are widely divergent, non-noble metals are used, or ligands or templates independently control morphology.
Failure of the rapid-pulse condition to improve elemental homogeneity relative to the slower-profile control would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
